newsitem.title: USA: Rockwell Chairman to retire after decade of change.
newsitem.headline: Rockwell Chairman to retire after decade of change.

text.p: Rockwell International Corp. Chairman and Chief Executive Don Beall announced his retirement on Wednesday after leading the company through a decade of transformation.

Beall, 58, said in a statement that he plans to step down as chief executive on Sept. 30, at the end of the company's current fiscal year, and as chairman in February, after Rockwell's annual shareholder meeting.
Beall, who first joined Rockwell in 1968, will remain as a company director and will be chairman of a new executive committee.
He will be succeeded by Don Davis Jr., Rockwell's president and chief operating officer.

"Now that we have completed the major steps in the strategic transformation of Rockwell into a highly focused electronics company, it is an appropriate time for me to turn the reins over to Don Davis," Beall said.
"I feel privileged to have led Rockwell over these years and will continue to be available to assist in any way possible," he said.
Beall has been chairman and chief executive since 1988. Before that, he served as president and chief operating officer from 1979 to 1988.

"Don Beall has set a high standard indeed," Davis said. "For nearly 20 years he has brought great strategic insight and visionary leadership to Rockwell, and nowhere is this better exemplified than in the area of enhanced shareowner value."

During his tenure, Beall transformed Seal Beach-based Rockwell from a defence and aerospace conglomerate reliant on government spending to a highly profitable electronics business. In 1984, some 63 percent of Rockwell's sales came from the U.S. government, compared with just 7 percent today.
During the past decade, the defence industry underwent rapid consolidation as the government's defence budget shrunk.
Through a series of acquisitions and divestitures, Rockwell became an electronics company specialising in industrial automation systems, semiconductors and avionics and communications equipment.
A major part of Rockwell's change took place last December, when it sold its defence and aerospace businesses to Boeing Co. for $3.2 billion.

Since 1984, Rockwell's earnings per share have increased at an annual rate of 19 percent. Beall's strategy was to sell off or restructure slow-growth businesses while acquiring and expanding the high-technology businesses where earnings growth potential was greater.
Beall also worked to build the international side of Rockwell's business. Almost 40 percent of Rockwell's sales now come from overseas; the company is active in more than 100 countries.

Rockwell's products are as diverse as landing systems for aircraft, global positioning system (GPS) receivers, high-speed, 56-kilobit-per-second modem chip sets; and 1automation systems used from factories to stage shows.
